lead: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is how a browser and server talk: the client sends a request, the server replies, and the server remembers nothing between messages. That statelessness is why every request must carry all the server needs. HTTPS is the same conversation inside TLS, so the path cannot read it. Every app — IRCTC, UPI, a result page — is a stream of these messages. This chapter reads one request and response line by line, then sorts methods and status codes by their promises.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for URLs and DNS, and 1.2 for the client-server exchange.

sections.h3: One URL, one request, one response

blocks.text: A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) names one resource on one host. In https://api.example.com/items/7?expand=price the scheme is https; host api.example.com is resolved by DNS (1.1); port is omitted and defaults to 443 for HTTPS, 80 for HTTP; path /items/7 names the resource; query ?expand=price carries input. A #fragment stays in the browser.

In HTTP/1.1 the message is plain text (ASCII headers); HTTP/2 sends the same information in a binary frame format, covered in Section 4. A request has four parts: request line (method, path with query, version), header lines Name: value, one compulsory empty line, then optional body. A response has a status line (version, three-digit code, reason phrase), headers, empty line, optional body.

blocks.code:
GET /items/7?expand=price HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Accept: application/json
// empty line; GET has no body

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 84
// empty line, then 84 bytes of JSON

blocks.text: HTTP is stateless: the server keeps no memory of earlier requests, so each one must carry its own identity, format and parameters. Cookies, sessions and tokens add memory on top (Unit 4, Cookies and session tracking).

sections.h3: Methods: the verb of the request

blocks.text: The method names the action. A method is safe when it only reads and does not change server state. A method is idempotent when sending the same request twice leaves the same end state as sending it once.

The table's safe methods are GET, HEAD and OPTIONS; the standard also defines TRACE as safe, rarely used in app code. GET is the everyday read: typing an address, clicking a link, an HttpClient.get() call (Unit 5) sends GET. POST submits data and changes state, so it is neither safe nor idempotent — a double click on Pay in a UPI app can create two orders. PUT replaces the whole resource, so repeating it is harmless. DELETE repeated is harmless; the second call may answer 404. PATCH sends a partial update and is not idempotent in general. HEAD returns headers with no body. OPTIONS asks which methods a resource allows; browsers use it before a cross-origin request.
The status code is three digits; the first digit is the class.

items: 1xx — informational; the request is still in progress (100 Continue).
2xx — success; the request was understood and done.
3xx — redirection; the resource is elsewhere or unchanged.
4xx — client error; the request itself is wrong.
5xx — server error; the request was fine and the server failed.

head: Code
Meaning
rows: new resource made; Location header points to it
new URL in Location; update your links
your cached copy is still valid
no such resource on this server

blocks.text: The reason phrase is for humans and may say anything; only the code is guaranteed. The class tells you who must act: on a 4xx fix the request, on a 5xx retry later or report a bug.
HTTP/1.1 keeps the TCP connection open after a response — a persistent connection — so requests reuse it one after another. Pipelining proved fragile, so browsers open about six connections per host.
HTTP/2 multiplexes many independent streams on one TCP connection, compresses headers and is binary, which cuts latency. TCP still delivers bytes in order, so one lost packet stalls every stream.
HTTP/3 runs on QUIC over UDP, so a lost packet stalls only its own stream and the handshake is shorter.
HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS on port 443. TLS encrypts bytes, detects tampering, and proves server identity with a certificate, so an OTP on café Wi-Fi is unreadable on the path.
For live traffic — chat, a cricket score ticker, a game — request-response is clumsy. WebSockets keep one two-way connection open; WebRTC carries peer-to-peer media and data.

figure.caption: The chapter's worked example in order: GET /items/7?expand=price gets 200 OK with an 84-byte body, POST /items gets 201 Created, DELETE /items/7 gets 204 No Content with 0 bytes. Notice all three codes are 2xx success, and only 204 forbids a body.

spec.aria: A client sends GET /items/7?expand=price and gets 200 OK with an 84-byte body, sends POST /items and gets 201 Created with a Location header, then sends DELETE /items/7 and gets 204 No Content with a 0-byte body.

examples.question: A client sends GET /items/7?expand=price HTTP/1.1 to api.example.com on port 443. The reply is HTTP/1.1 200 OK, Content-Type: application/json, Content-Length: 84. Then POST /items returns 201 Created; then DELETE /items/7 returns 204 No Content. (a) Classify each status code. (b) Is GET safe and idempotent? (c) Give the body length of the GET and DELETE replies.
steps: First digits 2, 2, 2: all three are 2xx success.
200 OK has a body; 201 Created reports a new resource with Location; 204 No Content sends no body by design.
GET reads only, so it is safe; repeating gives the same state, so it is idempotent.
Content-Length: 84 means GET body is 84 bytes; 204 forbids a body, so DELETE body is 0 bytes.
examples.answer: All three are 2xx success; GET is safe and idempotent; GET body = 84 bytes, DELETE body = 0 bytes.
examples.check:
get_body = 84
delete_body = 0
print('GET body =', get_body, 'bytes')
print('DELETE body =', delete_body, 'bytes')
examples.output:
GET body = 84 bytes
DELETE body = 0 bytes

examples.question: A browser requests http://shop.example.com/old and gets HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently with Location: https://shop.example.com/new. It follows that URL; a later PUT /orders/7 returns 204 No Content. (a) What class are 301 and 204? (b) What does Location do? (c) How many bytes of body does the 204 reply carry?
steps: 301 starts with 3: redirection. 204 starts with 2: success.
Location gives the new URL; the client must request that URL.
204 No Content means success with no body, so 0 bytes.
examples.answer: 301 is 3xx redirection; 204 is 2xx success; Location names the new URL; 204 body = 0 bytes.
examples.check:
code = 301
body = 0
print('301 class = 3xx')
print('204 class = 2xx')
print('204 body =', body, 'bytes')

traps: Safe is not zero side effects: GET may be logged or counted but must not change the resource. The table's safe methods are GET, HEAD and OPTIONS; the standard also defines TRACE as safe, rarely used in app code.

POST and PATCH are the common methods that are neither safe nor idempotent. Retrying a POST after a timeout can create a duplicate order; PATCH may also give a different result when repeated. Retrying PUT or DELETE cannot create a duplicate.
401 and 403 look alike: 401 means you are not authenticated or your credentials are wrong; 403 means you are known but not allowed. A login page often returns 401.
404 is a client-side problem (wrong URL); 500 is the server failing after a valid request. Never blame the client for a 5xx.
301 and 304 both start with 3 and involve the browser: 301 sends you to a new URL, 304 tells you to reuse your cached copy with no body sent.

quiz.q: Name the table's safe methods and say what safe means. Which other standard method is safe but rare in app code?
quiz.a: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS; the standard also defines TRACE as safe. Safe means reads only, no change to server state.

quiz.q: What does a 5xx status code mean?
quiz.a: Server error: the request was valid but the server failed, as in 500 Internal Server Error.

quiz.q: Why must a stateless protocol resend the login token on every request?
quiz.a: The server keeps no memory between requests, so each request must carry its own identity, usually a cookie or token header.

quiz.q: Why does HTTP/2 need multiplexing when HTTP/1.1 already has persistent connections?
quiz.a: Persistent connections still handle requests one after another; a slow response blocks the queue. Multiplexing interleaves many streams on one connection.

quiz.q: A script sends PUT /items/7 three times after timeouts, then DELETE /items/7 twice. What is the end state and why is retry safe?
quiz.a: PUT is idempotent: three replacements equal one. DELETE is idempotent: the item ends removed; the second may answer 404. No duplicate resources.

quiz.q: A request reaches a server with a wrong path, then the database crashes. Which single code fits each case?
quiz.a: Wrong path: 404 Not Found, a 4xx client error. Database crash: 500 Internal Server Error, a 5xx server error.

quiz.q: A mobile app retries every failed request once. Which methods can duplicate data? How do you stop that?
quiz.a: POST and PATCH can duplicate: two POSTs create two orders, repeated PATCH may differ. Retry only safe or idempotent methods, or send POST with a unique idempotency key the server checks first.

quiz.q: A page uses HTTPS, yet a colleague says traffic can still be modified on public Wi-Fi. What does TLS guarantee and what does it not?
quiz.a: TLS encrypts bytes, detects tampering, and authenticates the server by certificate, so the path cannot read or silently change the request. It does not protect a compromised device, a wrong host name, or data after the server.

beyond: Not for the exam. Large content networks serve over HTTP/3 on QUIC because the shorter handshake copes with lossy mobile links. gRPC requires HTTP/2 framing; GraphQL is transport-agnostic but is usually sent as a single POST to one endpoint, so the methods and status codes still apply. WebSockets carry chat and live scores; WebRTC carries video calls in the browser. Search RFC 9110 for HTTP semantics and RFC 9000 for QUIC. TLS 1.3 and post-quantum key exchange are where transport security is heading.
